pages.text:
*The Eighteenth Rule of Mapmaking: Let the reader check your work.*

Runners in blue livery swept across the hall, their feet slapping the stone floor with a rhythmic thud that echoed off the high vaulted ceiling. They carried the two most contested maps, Tam’s rough, ink-stained parchment and Lucan’s pristine, gold-leafed sheet, toward the massive oak shelves at the rear of the room. There, rolled in dust and time, lay the Guild’s oldest sketches of the Marches, drawn by hands long dead.

Guildmaster Quint unrolled the ancient papers with a reverence that made the air feel thinner. He held Lucan’s map up to the light. It showed a flat, green meadow where the Greywater marsh squelched. He looked at the old sketch. It showed mud. He looked at Lucan. He did not smile.

Then he turned to Tam’s map. It was crooked, blotchy, and smelled faintly of pine resin. It showed a sunk road, a cluster of broken stones, and a dark, reedy expanse that matched the old sketch perfectly. The truth was there, ugly and undeniable, while the beauty was a lie. The hall held its breath, waiting to see which map would be called a map.
pages.image: Guildmaster Quint, a tall man in robes, compares a pristine gold-leafed map with a rough, ink-stained parchment against ancient rolled scrolls on a high wooden shelf in a dim, vaulted hall.

pages.text:
Before anyone could speak, Lucan Ravel stepped forward. His green coat was immaculate, but his hands were trembling at his sides. He looked at his father, Lord Ravel, who sat in the front row with his face tight as a drum. Then Lucan looked at the Guildmaster.

"My map is wrong," Lucan said. His voice shook, but it carried to the back of the room. "I drew the Greywater from the ridge. I never walked it. I trusted the old charts because they were pretty." He swallowed, his throat working. "My team nearly drowned. Tamsin Marrow pulled us out."

A murmur rippled through the apprentices, a sound like wind through dry reeds. Lord Ravel went pale, then a strange, slow softening spread across his stern features. He did not look away from his son. He did not look at Tam. He simply sat there, holding the truth in his lap, a burden heavier than any gold compass he had ever owned.
pages.image: Lucan Ravel, a boy in a green coat, stands in the center of a stone hall with his hands trembling, looking up at a stern man in the front row while other apprentices watch in shock.

pages.text:
"The Guild has always valued craft," Quint said, his voice low and steady. "But today, we ask for growth. Show us how you improved."

The Academy apprentices stepped up one by one. They spoke of lens glass, of new inks that did not bleed, of geometric perfection. Their maps were beautiful, flawless, and static. Then it was Tam’s turn. She walked to the table, her patched coat rustling. She did not take out a ruler. She took out the small, stitched notebook.

The Yesterday Book.

She opened it on the judges' table, her ink-stained fingers careful and gentle. She turned to the first page, a week after the Survey began. A river wobbled there, crooked and thick, like a snake that had fallen off a cart. She turned the page. Another river, slightly straighter. She turned another. The lines grew cleaner, the bends more deliberate. She showed them the week the rain ruined her work, where the pages were damp and the lines smudged. Then she showed them the last page.
pages.image: Tam Marrow, a girl in a brown patched coat, opens a small stitched notebook on a wooden table, revealing pages of hand-drawn wobbly lines, while Guildmaster Quint watches closely.

pages.text:
"This is not a map of the land," Tam said. Her voice was small, but it did not waver. "It is a map of me."

She looked up, her cheeks burning red. "I am not a good mapmaker yet. I blot. I crook. I started further behind than anyone in this room. I learned to read at nine, on the docks, with a man who smelled of fish glue. I have no silver buttons. I have no gold compass."

She closed the book, not with a thud, but with a soft click. "But I am a better one than I was on the first day. And I will be a better one tomorrow. That is the only promise I can keep."

The silence in the great hall was heavy, like a wet wool blanket dropped over a head. It was the quiet that follows when a child stops reciting a lesson and simply tells the truth. The Guildmaster stared at the small stitched notebook, then at Tam’s ink-stained fingers, and for a moment the room seemed to hold its tongue, waiting to see if the girl would say something more. She did not. She simply stood there, her patched coat rustling faintly in the still air, and the beautiful, flawless maps of the Academy apprentices suddenly looked very much like drawings of birds that had never learned to fly.
pages.image: Tam Marrow stands before a large wooden table, her face flushed, holding a small closed notebook, while Guildmaster Quint and other judges lean forward in the dim light of the hall.

pages.text:
Guildmaster Quint reached out, his hand steady despite his age, and picked up the Yesterday Book. He did not look at the judges. Nor at the other apprentices. His gaze fixed instead on the old woman in the corner, the one with the bandaged ankle and the lavender scarf, who watched with eyes that were suddenly, sharply bright.

He turned the pages slowly. One. Two. Three. The crooked river appeared, then the straighter one, followed by the smudged week. Finally, there was the clean line. He traced the ink with his fingertip, a whisper of a gesture, touching the respect that lay beneath the surface. For a long, long moment, he said nothing. The dust motes danced in the shaft of light falling from the high window.

Then he looked up, his gaze finding Odalys Finch.

"Odalys," he said quietly, and the word hung in the air, warm and heavy. "You were right."
pages.image: Guildmaster Quint holds a small stitched notebook in his hands, his finger tracing a line, while looking at an old woman with white hair in a bun and a lavender scarf sitting in a wooden chair.
